title: CASE and conditional logic
summary_md: Branching inside a query: searched vs simple CASE, evaluation order and type rules, IF/IIF/COALESCE/NULLIF, bucketing, conditional-aggregation pivots, and custom sorting.

sections.heading: Searched vs simple CASE
sections.body_md:
- **Searched CASE**: each WHEN is a full boolean condition. Most flexible; use it by default.
- **Simple CASE**: compares one expression to values with `=`. Shorter for lookups, but it **cannot match NULL** (`WHEN NULL` is never true).
- First WHEN that is TRUE wins; if none match you get the ELSE value, or **NULL** if there is no ELSE.
- CASE is an expression: it returns a value and can appear in SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY, ORDER BY, and inside aggregates.
- Always close with `END`. Give the result an alias.

syntax.mysql:
CASE WHEN cond1 THEN r1 [WHEN cond2 THEN r2 ...] [ELSE r_else] END
CASE expr WHEN v1 THEN r1 [WHEN v2 THEN r2 ...] [ELSE r_else] END
syntax.tsql:
CASE WHEN cond1 THEN r1 [WHEN cond2 THEN r2 ...] [ELSE r_else] END
CASE expr WHEN v1 THEN r1 [WHEN v2 THEN r2 ...] [ELSE r_else] END

args.name: WHEN cond
args.meaning: Boolean condition (searched form) or value compared to expr with = (simple form).

args.name: THEN r
args.meaning: Value returned when that WHEN matches.

args.name: ELSE r_else
args.meaning: Value when nothing matches; omitted means NULL.

args.name: expr
args.meaning: Simple form only: the single expression compared to each WHEN value.

examples.title: Searched CASE: salary bands
examples.explain_md: Order the conditions from most to least specific. Jon (NULL salary) must be handled first or he falls into ELSE.
examples.mysql:
SELECT name, salary,
       CASE WHEN salary IS NULL     THEN 'unknown'
            WHEN salary >= 150000   THEN 'senior'
            WHEN salary >= 90000    THEN 'mid'
            ELSE 'junior'
       END AS band
FROM employees
ORDER BY emp_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT name, salary,
       CASE WHEN salary IS NULL     THEN 'unknown'
            WHEN salary >= 150000   THEN 'senior'
            WHEN salary >= 90000    THEN 'mid'
            ELSE 'junior'
       END AS band
FROM employees
ORDER BY emp_id;

examples.title: Simple CASE: map codes to labels
examples.explain_md: Equality lookup against one column. Unlisted departments return NULL because there is no ELSE.
examples.mysql:
SELECT name, dept,
       CASE dept WHEN 'Engineering' THEN 'ENG'
                 WHEN 'Sales'       THEN 'SLS'
                 WHEN 'Marketing'   THEN 'MKT'
       END AS code
FROM employees
ORDER BY emp_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT name, dept,
       CASE dept WHEN 'Engineering' THEN 'ENG'
                 WHEN 'Sales'       THEN 'SLS'
                 WHEN 'Marketing'   THEN 'MKT'
       END AS code
FROM employees
ORDER BY emp_id;

examples.title: Simple CASE cannot test NULL
examples.explain_md: `CASE salary WHEN NULL` compiles to `salary = NULL`, never true. Jon lands in ELSE; the searched form with IS NULL is correct.
examples.mysql:
SELECT name,
       CASE salary WHEN NULL THEN 'no salary' ELSE 'has salary' END AS wrong_check,
       CASE WHEN salary IS NULL THEN 'no salary' ELSE 'has salary' END AS right_check
FROM employees
WHERE emp_id IN (9, 10)
ORDER BY emp_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT name,
       CASE salary WHEN NULL THEN 'no salary' ELSE 'has salary' END AS wrong_check,
       CASE WHEN salary IS NULL THEN 'no salary' ELSE 'has salary' END AS right_check
FROM employees
WHERE emp_id IN (9, 10)
ORDER BY emp_id;

pitfalls_md: Forgetting ELSE yields NULL, which then vanishes from SUM/AVG or breaks `<>` filters downstream.

sections.heading: Order of evaluation and result types
sections.body_md:
- WHENs are tested **top to bottom**; the first TRUE one wins and the rest are ignored. Overlapping ranges therefore depend on order.
- Put the most specific / narrowest condition first, and NULL handling before comparisons.
- All THEN/ELSE results must share a compatible type. MySQL coerces silently; SQL Server picks the highest-precedence type and errors if a string cannot convert (`THEN 1 ... ELSE 'n/a'` fails).
- Do not rely on CASE to prevent a divide-by-zero in SQL Server when aggregates appear inside it; use `NULLIF(denominator, 0)`.
- CASE branches are not guaranteed to be evaluated lazily in every situation; keep branch expressions side-effect free.

examples.title: Wrong order: broad condition first
examples.explain_md: `salary >= 0` is true for everyone with a salary, so the later branches never run.
examples.mysql:
SELECT name, salary,
       CASE WHEN salary >= 0      THEN 'junior'
            WHEN salary >= 90000  THEN 'mid'
            WHEN salary >= 150000 THEN 'senior'
       END AS band
FROM employees
WHERE emp_id IN (1, 2, 5, 10)
ORDER BY emp_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT name, salary,
       CASE WHEN salary >= 0      THEN 'junior'
            WHEN salary >= 90000  THEN 'mid'
            WHEN salary >= 150000 THEN 'senior'
       END AS band
FROM employees
WHERE emp_id IN (1, 2, 5, 10)
ORDER BY emp_id;

examples.title: Right order: narrowest first
examples.explain_md: Check from the top threshold down, so each row meets the highest band it qualifies for.
examples.mysql:
SELECT name, salary,
       CASE WHEN salary >= 150000 THEN 'senior'
            WHEN salary >= 90000  THEN 'mid'
            WHEN salary >= 0      THEN 'junior'
       END AS band
FROM employees
WHERE emp_id IN (1, 2, 5, 10)
ORDER BY emp_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT name, salary,
       CASE WHEN salary >= 150000 THEN 'senior'
            WHEN salary >= 90000  THEN 'mid'
            WHEN salary >= 0      THEN 'junior'
       END AS band
FROM employees
WHERE emp_id IN (1, 2, 5, 10)
ORDER BY emp_id;

examples.title: Keep branch types consistent
examples.explain_md: Cast the number so every branch is text. Mixing `salary` (int) with `'n/a'` raises a conversion error in SQL Server.
examples.mysql:
SELECT name,
       CASE WHEN salary IS NULL THEN 'n/a'
            ELSE CAST(salary AS CHAR(10)) END AS salary_text
FROM employees
WHERE emp_id IN (9, 10)
ORDER BY emp_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT name,
       CASE WHEN salary IS NULL THEN 'n/a'
            ELSE CAST(salary AS VARCHAR(10)) END AS salary_text
FROM employees
WHERE emp_id IN (9, 10)
ORDER BY emp_id;
examples.dialect_note_md: MySQL's `CAST(x AS CHAR(n))` is `CAST(x AS VARCHAR(n))` in SQL Server.

sections.heading: IF() and IIF(), COALESCE, NULLIF
sections.body_md:
- Two-way shortcut: MySQL `IF(cond, then, else)`, SQL Server `IIF(cond, then, else)`. Both are just a one-WHEN CASE.
- CASE is the portable choice and the one to write on a whiteboard.
- `COALESCE(a, b, c)` returns the first non-NULL argument (portable). MySQL `IFNULL(a, b)` and SQL Server `ISNULL(a, b)` are the two-argument versions.
- `NULLIF(a, b)` returns NULL when a = b, else a. Useful to avoid /0 or to turn '' or 0 into NULL.
- `ISNULL` in SQL Server takes the type of the first argument (can truncate); COALESCE uses precedence of all arguments.

syntax.mysql: IF(cond, then_val, else_val)   IFNULL(a, b)   COALESCE(a, b, ...)   NULLIF(a, b)
syntax.tsql: IIF(cond, then_val, else_val)   ISNULL(a, b)   COALESCE(a, b, ...)   NULLIF(a, b)

args.name: else_val
args.meaning: Returned when cond is FALSE or UNKNOWN (NULL).

args.name: a, b, ...
args.meaning: COALESCE: tried left to right, first non-NULL wins.

args.name: NULLIF(a, b)
args.meaning: NULL if a equals b, otherwise a.

examples.title: One-line flag
examples.explain_md: MySQL spells it IF, SQL Server IIF.
examples.mysql:
SELECT name, IF(salary >= 100000, 'yes', 'no') AS high_earner
FROM employees
WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY emp_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT name, IIF(salary >= 100000, 'yes', 'no') AS high_earner
FROM employees
WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY emp_id;
examples.dialect_note_md: `IF()` exists only in MySQL; `IIF()` exists only in SQL Server (2012+). `CASE WHEN salary >= 100000 THEN 'yes' ELSE 'no' END` works in both.

examples.title: COALESCE and NULLIF
examples.explain_md: COALESCE supplies a default for Jon's NULL salary; `NULLIF(salary, 80000)` turns Gus's 80000 into NULL and leaves other values alone.
examples.mysql:
SELECT name,
       COALESCE(salary, 0)  AS salary_or_zero,
       NULLIF(salary, 80000) AS salary_hide_80k
FROM employees
WHERE emp_id IN (7, 9, 10)
ORDER BY emp_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT name,
       COALESCE(salary, 0)  AS salary_or_zero,
       NULLIF(salary, 80000) AS salary_hide_80k
FROM employees
WHERE emp_id IN (7, 9, 10)
ORDER BY emp_id;

sections.heading: Bucketing with CASE
sections.body_md:
- Turn a continuous value into labelled ranges, then `GROUP BY` the label.
- Compute the label in a derived table / CTE so the CASE is written once (SQL Server cannot GROUP BY the alias).
- Use consistent boundaries: `>= low AND < high` so no value falls in two buckets.
- Add an ordering key so buckets sort logically, not alphabetically.
- To show buckets that have zero rows, you need a bucket list to LEFT JOIN from.

examples.title: Order size buckets
examples.explain_md: Count and total by size band. The numeric `ord` column drives a sensible sort.
examples.mysql:
SELECT ord, bucket, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM (
  SELECT amount,
         CASE WHEN amount < 50  THEN 1
              WHEN amount < 100 THEN 2
              ELSE 3 END AS ord,
         CASE WHEN amount < 50  THEN 'small (<50)'
              WHEN amount < 100 THEN 'medium (50-99)'
              ELSE 'large (100+)' END AS bucket
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'completed'
) AS b
GROUP BY ord, bucket
ORDER BY ord;
examples.tsql:
SELECT ord, bucket, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM (
  SELECT amount,
         CASE WHEN amount < 50  THEN 1
              WHEN amount < 100 THEN 2
              ELSE 3 END AS ord,
         CASE WHEN amount < 50  THEN 'small (<50)'
              WHEN amount < 100 THEN 'medium (50-99)'
              ELSE 'large (100+)' END AS bucket
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'completed'
) AS b
GROUP BY ord, bucket
ORDER BY ord;

examples.title: Hire-year cohort
examples.explain_md: CASE on a date column using half-open boundaries.
examples.mysql:
SELECT cohort, COUNT(*) AS people
FROM (
  SELECT CASE WHEN hire_date < '2019-01-01' THEN 'before 2019'
              WHEN hire_date < '2022-01-01' THEN '2019-2021'
              ELSE '2022+' END AS cohort
  FROM employees
) AS t
GROUP BY cohort
ORDER BY cohort;
examples.tsql:
SELECT cohort, COUNT(*) AS people
FROM (
  SELECT CASE WHEN hire_date < '2019-01-01' THEN 'before 2019'
              WHEN hire_date < '2022-01-01' THEN '2019-2021'
              ELSE '2022+' END AS cohort
  FROM employees
) AS t
GROUP BY cohort
ORDER BY cohort;

sections.heading: Conditional aggregation as a pivot
sections.body_md:
- Rows to columns without PIVOT: one `SUM(CASE WHEN key = 'x' THEN value END)` per output column, `GROUP BY` the row key.
- The column list is fixed in the SQL (static pivot). A dynamic list needs generated SQL, which is outside plain SELECT.
- Missing combinations give NULL (no ELSE) or 0 (`ELSE 0`); wrap in COALESCE if you want zeros.
- The same trick works with `COUNT(CASE ... THEN 1 END)` for counts.

examples.title: Daily revenue with a column per region
examples.explain_md: One row per day. West has no row on 03-04, so its cell is NULL (no sales row existed).
examples.mysql:
SELECT sale_date,
       SUM(CASE WHEN region = 'East' THEN revenue END) AS east,
       SUM(CASE WHEN region = 'West' THEN revenue END) AS west
FROM daily_sales
WHERE sale_date <= '2024-03-05'
GROUP BY sale_date
ORDER BY sale_date;
examples.tsql:
SELECT sale_date,
       SUM(CASE WHEN region = 'East' THEN revenue END) AS east,
       SUM(CASE WHEN region = 'West' THEN revenue END) AS west
FROM daily_sales
WHERE sale_date <= '2024-03-05'
GROUP BY sale_date
ORDER BY sale_date;

examples.title: Order amount per customer by status
examples.explain_md: Each status becomes a column; COALESCE makes absent combinations 0.
examples.mysql:
SELECT customer_id,
       COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'completed' THEN amount END), 0) AS completed,
       COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'cancelled' THEN amount END), 0) AS cancelled,
       COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'refunded'  THEN amount END), 0) AS refunded
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY customer_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT customer_id,
       COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'completed' THEN amount END), 0) AS completed,
       COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'cancelled' THEN amount END), 0) AS cancelled,
       COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'refunded'  THEN amount END), 0) AS refunded
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY customer_id;

sections.heading: CASE in ORDER BY (custom sort)
sections.body_md:
- Sort by a rank you define: `ORDER BY CASE col WHEN 'a' THEN 1 WHEN 'b' THEN 2 ELSE 3 END`.
- **NULLs last**: MySQL and SQL Server sort NULLs *first* ascending and *last* descending, and neither has `NULLS LAST`. Use `ORDER BY CASE WHEN col IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END, col`.
- Put a final tiebreak (an id) after the CASE keys so the order is fully deterministic.
- The CASE does not need to be in the SELECT list (except with `SELECT DISTINCT` in SQL Server).

examples.title: Pin a status order
examples.explain_md: Business order, not alphabetical: completed, then refunded, then cancelled.
examples.mysql:
SELECT order_id, status
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id IN (1, 4)
ORDER BY CASE status WHEN 'completed' THEN 1
                     WHEN 'refunded'  THEN 2
                     ELSE 3 END,
         order_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT order_id, status
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id IN (1, 4)
ORDER BY CASE status WHEN 'completed' THEN 1
                     WHEN 'refunded'  THEN 2
                     ELSE 3 END,
         order_id;

examples.title: Salary descending, NULL last
examples.explain_md: A plain ascending sort would put Jon's NULL first; the leading CASE key pushes NULLs last in both dialects.
examples.mysql:
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY CASE WHEN salary IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END,
         salary,
         emp_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY CASE WHEN salary IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END,
         salary,
         emp_id;

examples.title: Pin one value to the top
examples.explain_md: Sales first, then everything else alphabetically by department, then by id.
